section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section provides the header information for the maamar, including the Torah portion and date.
section.t: With the help of Heaven.
Shabbat of Haazinu,
Shabbat Shuvah, 5740*

section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section introduces the verse "Return O Israel until Hashem your G-d" and questions the specific wording and the use of the two Divine names.
section.t: "Return O Israel until Hashem your G-d"1,
And it is known regarding this the precise point of our Nesi'im: what is the meaning of saying "until Hashem your G-d," for seemingly it should have said "to Hashem your G-d"2.
And also the fact that it uses the two names Havayah and Elokecha3.
And especially since it says here "Return O Israel,"
for the name Israel describes the highest level within Israel,
for the Children of Israel are generally divided into two levels: Yaakov and Israel,
and the name Israel is because "you have striven with G-d and with men and have prevailed"4,
from which it is understood that it speaks here about the matter of the completeness of teshuvah5.
And as is also understood from the fact that the haftarah of Shabbat Teshuvah is "Shuvah Yisrael,"
that the teshuvah of Shabbat Teshuvah is a lofty level of teshuvah ila'ah.
For behold, Shabbat, the letters of which spell "tashev" (you shall return), is the aspect of teshuvah ila'ah6,
And within teshuvah ila'ah itself
[which has several levels]
it is a lofty teshuvah, for one must be all his days
(even on weekdays)
in teshuvah ila'ah7,
from which it is understood,
that Shabbat is a lofty level within teshuvah ila'ah itself.
And especially on Shabbat Teshuvah, which rectifies and elevates all the Shabbats of the year
[as explained in the writings of the Arizal8
regarding the seven days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, which contain all seven days of the week,
that on the first day of the week within these days, they rectify and elevate all the Sundays of the entire year,
and likewise on the second day, etc.,
and on Shabbat Teshuvah they rectify and elevate all the Shabbats of the entire year],
for the teshuvah of Shabbat Teshuvah is loftier even than the teshuvah of all the Shabbats of the year,
and this teshuvah is analogous to Yom Kippur9
about which it is written10
"For on this day He shall atone for you... before Hashem you shall be purified,"
"before Hashem" specifically, above the name Havayah11,
and even more than this it says "He shall atone for you" simply, referring to the One who has no known name and is not grasped by any name, etc.12,
So why does it say here "until Hashem your G-d"?

section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that "Return until Hashem your G-d" refers to the unification of Havayah and Elokim, a higher knowledge achieved through teshuvah, as opposed to the service of tzaddikim.
section.t: And the explanation of this is known13,
that what is written "Return O Israel until Hashem your G-d" is the matter of the unification of Havayah and Elokim, as it is written14
"And you shall know... that Havayah, He is Elokim,"
which is a most lofty knowledge,
as explained in the Zohar15.
And therefore it says "Return O Israel until Hashem your G-d," because the matter of teshuvah is connected to this knowledge, as it is written16
(regarding the matter of teshuvah that was on Mount Carmel)
"And they said, 'Hashem, He is Elokim; Hashem, He is Elokim.'"
And the repetition of "Hashem, He is Elokim; Hashem, He is Elokim" twice is because through the service of teshuvah,
which is above the service of tzaddikim,
the matter of "Hashem, He is Elokim" is drawn down twice.
And as it is brought in the Midrash17
"At Sinai it was said18
'I am Hashem your G-d'; at Carmel it was said doubly, 'Hashem, He is Elokim; Hashem, He is Elokim,'"
And it is explained in Likkutei Torah19
that at Sinai, Israel was on the level of tzaddikim,
and through the service of tzaddikim
(the performance of mitzvos)
the matter of "Hashem, He is Elokim" was drawn down once,
but at Mount Carmel, through teshuvah, they drew down "Hashem, He is Elokim" twice.
And this is similar to what at the Giving of the Torah is written "I am Hashem your G-d,"
"I am" once,
but regarding teshuvah it is written20
"I, I am He... for My sake...,"
"I" twice,
because through the service of performing mitzvos, the aspect of "I" is drawn down once,
but the drawing down through the service of teshuvah is higher than the drawing down through the service of performing mitzvos21.
For this is also the meaning of "I, I am He... for My sake," and Targum renders it "for the sake of My name,"
up to the aspect of His great name22,
and higher still, the aspect of "He and His name alone,"
before the tzimtzum.
